title: Cello Suite No. 1 in G major, BWV 1007: I. Prélude
recordingNote: From 'Six Evolutions – Bach: Cello Suites' (2018), Ma's third recording of the complete suites; official Sony video on the YoYoMaVEVO channel
context: Bach wrote his six cello suites sometime between 1717 and 1723 while working as Kapellmeister at Köthen; the exact dating is uncertain. They were little performed in the modern era until Pablo Casals began recording them in 1936. Yo-Yo Ma has recorded the complete set three times, most recently for Six Evolutions (2018), the source of this official video. The Prélude is built almost entirely from one repeated pattern of broken chords — a single idea, worked patiently for about two and a half minutes.
listenFor: How the same arpeggio pattern seems to change colour every time it returns, even though nothing about it changes.

title: The Four Seasons, No. 2 'Summer' in G minor, RV 315: III. Presto
recordingNote: Live concert recording from April 2022 at the Esplanade Concert Hall, Singapore; from Chua's Pentatone debut album 'Vivaldi: Four Seasons / Locatelli: Harmonic Labyrinth' (2023)
context: Vivaldi's Four Seasons were published in Amsterdam in 1725 as the first four concertos of Il cimento dell'armonia e dell'inventione, each paired with a sonnet describing the music. The Presto that closes Summer is a storm: slashing rain figures and sudden thunder. Violinist Chloe Chua won joint first prize at the 2018 Yehudi Menuhin Competition playing 'Winter', aged 11. This performance with the Singapore Symphony was filmed live when she was 15.
listenFor: The violins' slashing figure — Vivaldi's musical hail — answered by the orchestra's low thunder rolls.

title: Piano Trio in G minor, Op. 17
recordingNote: ATOS Trio's 2019 recording for the album 'Clara Schumann & Fanny Mendelssohn: Piano Trios'; full performance video on YouTube
context: Clara Schumann wrote her only piano trio in 1846, in Dresden, during a difficult stretch: her husband Robert was unwell, and she composed it while pregnant and made to rest. She later judged it harshly herself, but Robert's own Piano Trio in D minor, written the following year, responds to hers directly — her work shaped his. The ATOS Trio (Annette von Hehn, Stefan Heinemeyer, Thomas Hoppe) recorded it in 2019 for an album pairing Clara's trio with Fanny Mendelssohn's.
listenFor: The quiet, searching theme the piano opens with, and how the strings take it up and answer it back.

title: Symphony No. 7 in A major, Op. 92: II. Allegretto
recordingNote: Deutsche Grammophon recording of Beethoven's Symphonies Nos. 7 & 8, Abbado conducting the Vienna Philharmonic (℗ 1988)
context: Beethoven finished his Seventh Symphony in 1812 and conducted the first performance himself in Vienna on 8 December 1813, at a concert benefiting soldiers wounded at the Battle of Hanau. The second movement's insistently repeated rhythm — two short beats and one long — has made it one of the most recognisable things Beethoven wrote, and a fixture of film soundtracks. This recording pairs Claudio Abbado with the Vienna Philharmonic for Deutsche Grammophon.
listenFor: The ostinato pattern — two quick notes and one long — as it moves from the low strings up through the rest of the orchestra.

title: Suite bergamasque, L. 75: III. Clair de lune
recordingNote: From Cho's 2017 Deutsche Grammophon album 'Debussy'; music video filmed at the Siemensvilla, Berlin
context: Debussy began his Suite bergamasque around 1890, aged 28, and revised it heavily before publishing it in 1905. 'Clair de lune' had originally been titled 'Promenade sentimentale'; its final name comes from a Paul Verlaine poem, though the piece doesn't set the words. Seong-Jin Cho won the 2015 Chopin Competition and recorded Debussy's piano music for Deutsche Grammophon the following two years — this is the album's music video, filmed at Berlin's Siemensvilla.
listenFor: The pedal-blurred chords right at the opening, and the moment the melody finally settles back onto them.

title: Symphony No. 1 in E minor: III. Juba Dance. Allegro
recordingNote: From the Deutsche Grammophon album 'Florence Price: Symphonies Nos. 1 & 3' (2021)
context: Florence Price wrote her first symphony in 1931–32, partly while recovering from a broken foot, and it won the 1932 Wanamaker competition. On 15 June 1933 the Chicago Symphony Orchestra played it at the Century of Progress World's Fair — the first symphony by a Black woman performed by a major American orchestra. Instead of a conventional scherzo, the third movement is a Juba, after the body-percussion dance tradition of stamping, clapping and slapping.
listenFor: The percussion imitating clapping and stamping — plus a slide whistle turning up in the middle of a symphony.

title: D'un matin de printemps
recordingNote: Live concert video from the Seattle Symphony's official channel, Cristian Măcelaru conducting
context: Lili Boulanger wrote D'un matin de printemps between 1917 and early 1918, in the last year of her life — she died that March, aged 24. It was composed alongside D'un soir triste, a companion piece in a much darker mood, and both were premiered in Paris in 1921. In 1913 she had become the first woman to win the Prix de Rome for composition. This is a live performance from the Seattle Symphony, conducted by Cristian Măcelaru.
listenFor: The fluttering, almost buzzing figure the violins and woodwinds toss back and forth right at the opening.

title: Symphony No. 1 in G major, Op. 11, No. 1
recordingNote: Full live performance filmed in 2025, uploaded to the orchestra's official channel
context: Joseph Bologne, Chevalier de Saint-Georges, was born in Guadeloupe in 1745, the son of a French plantation owner and an enslaved African woman. He became one of 18th-century Paris's leading violinists and orchestra directors, and a champion fencer. His two symphonies Op. 11 were published in Paris in 1779. He is increasingly programmed by major orchestras; this is a complete live performance by the Lowell Chamber Orchestra.
listenFor: The opening Allegro's bright, tidy themes, and how often the orchestra hands the tune straight to the violins.

title: Spiegel im Spiegel (for cello and piano)
recordingNote: Cello-and-piano version recorded July 1995 at the Festeburgkirche, Frankfurt; released 1999 on ECM's album 'Alina'
context: Arvo Pärt wrote Spiegel im Spiegel in 1978, shortly before leaving Estonia, in the tintinnabuli style he had developed — a second voice built only from notes of the home chord, like bell overtones. This version, for cello and piano, was recorded in July 1995 at Frankfurt's Festeburgkirche and released in 1999 on ECM's album Alina. It has since been used in a long list of films and television shows.
listenFor: The cello line growing one note at a time, over and away from, the piano's bell-like triads.
restrictions: UMG auto-generated upload of the ECM recording — may behave differently in some embed contexts

title: On the Nature of Daylight (orchestral version)
recordingNote: Official audio of the 2016 orchestral version, released on Deutsche Grammophon for the album's anniversary reissue of 'The Blue Notebooks'
context: Max Richter wrote and recorded The Blue Notebooks in 2003; it was released the following year, and he has described the album as a protest against political, social and personal brutality. 'On the Nature of Daylight' is its best-known track, and it later turned up in films including Arrival. This is the 2016 orchestral version, an official Deutsche Grammophon audio release from the album's anniversary reissue.
listenFor: The sustained string chords looping underneath while the piano keeps circling the same small falling figure.

title: Barbara Allen
recordingNote: Her recording 'Barbry Ellen', released as official Smithsonian Folkways audio on the compilation Classic Mountain Songs (2002)
context: "Barbara Allen" is the most widely collected of all English-language folk ballads: the Vaughan Williams Memorial Library counts around 500 traditional recordings. The earliest is a 1907 wax cylinder made by Percy Grainger of the Lincolnshire singer Joseph Taylor. Jean Ritchie grew up singing in Viper, Kentucky, a tradition-bearer from an Appalachian family of singers, and her version keeps the ballad's plain, unadorned shape — a doomed young man, a hard-hearted woman, a letter read too late.
listenFor: The way Ritchie slows and holds the final line of each verse, a classic ballad-singer's trick before the story turns.

title: Goodnight, Irene
recordingNote: Official audio from the 2015 box set Lead Belly: The Smithsonian Folkways Collection
context: John Lomax first recorded Lead Belly singing "Irene" on a 1933 prison visit to Angola, Louisiana. Lead Belly said he learned the refrain from his uncle Terrill and may have sung it as a lullaby as early as 1908; it was published in 1936 as a joint Ledbetter–Lomax song. A year after his death in 1949, the Weavers' version topped the US charts for weeks, and Pete Seeger called it Lead Belly's theme song.
listenFor: The 12-string guitar rolling underneath a gentle 3/4 waltz beat.

title: This Land Is Your Land
recordingNote: Official Smithsonian Folkways upload from the 1997 collection The Asch Recordings, Vol. 1 (recordings made in the mid-1940s)
context: Guthrie wrote the words on 23 February 1940 in a New York hotel room, in irritated response to Kate Smith's "God Bless America" on the radio. The melody comes from the Carter Family's "When the World's on Fire". His April 1944 recording — the earliest known — includes the "private property" verse often left out of schoolbooks. In 2002 the Library of Congress added the song to the National Recording Registry.
listenFor: The tune is the Carter Family's "When the World's on Fire" — hear how little Guthrie changes it.

title: Wellerman
recordingNote: His 2021 single, the official NathanEvansVEVO visualiser upload
context: The "wellermen" were supply boats run by the Weller brothers, who set up a whaling station at Otago Heads, New Zealand, in 1831 and sold provisions to whalers. The song of the whaler waiting on "sugar and tea and rum" surfaced in print in New Zealand only in the 1970s, but in late 2020 a TikTok post by Scottish singer Nathan Evans turned it into a global hit and set off a sea-shanty craze.
listenFor: The call-and-response build, with stacked voices answering each line of the verse.

title: Seven Drunken Nights
recordingNote: Live at the Celtic Folk Festival Vienna, 1980, from the band's official YouTube channel
context: A version of the old song "Our Goodman" (Child 274), collected in Scotland in the 1770s: a drunkard comes home night after night to find fresh evidence of his wife's lover, and swallows each more implausible excuse. The Dubliners' 1967 single reached number 7 in the UK and number 1 in Ireland despite being kept off the air by broadcaster RTÉ for its ribald lyrics.
listenFor: The wife's excuses getting more absurd each verse — and the audience catching on before he does.

title: Elyne Road
recordingNote: Solo kora piece from his album The Mande Variations (World Circuit, 2008), official World Circuit Records audio
context: Toumani Diabaté (1965–2024) came from one of Mali's great hereditary griot families and played the 21-string kora. "Elyne Road" is an unaccompanied solo from The Mande Variations, his 2008 album of kora solos for World Circuit — no percussion, no vocals, just one instrument carrying bass line and melody at once. The official audio has drawn millions of plays and made the record a frequent gateway into West African music.
listenFor: Two hands doing entirely different jobs — a repeating bass pattern under a melody that keeps circling back.

title: Polegnala e Pschenitza (Harvest Song from Thrace)
recordingNote: From Le Mystère des Voix Bulgares, recorded by Marcel Cellier in 1975 and released on Nonesuch in 1987
context: The choir was founded in 1952 by Philip Koutev to showcase Bulgarian folk music and commission new arrangements of it. Swiss producer Marcel Cellier recorded them in 1975, and when Nonesuch issued the album in 1987 it set off worldwide interest; the follow-up volume won a 1989 Grammy for Best Traditional Folk Recording. This harvest song from Thrace is one of the album's shortest, brightest pieces.
listenFor: The deliberately wide, ringing harmonies — voices pitched just apart so they shimmer and beat against each other.

title: Llorando Se Fue
recordingNote: The original 1981 recording (from the album Canto a la mujer de mi pueblo), official KjarkasVEVO music video
context: Los Kjarkas, Bolivia's best-known Andean group, wrote and recorded this song in 1981, sung in Spanish over a slow, sad Afro-Bolivian saya rhythm and built on what Gonzalo Hermosa called a small, nostalgic Andean melody. In 1989 the French-Brazilian group Kaoma used the melody without permission for their dance hit "Lambada"; lawsuits followed, and the melody later resurfaced in hits like Jennifer Lopez's "On the Floor".
listenFor: The unhurried sway of the saya rhythm — a world away from the frantic Lambada it ended up feeding.

title: Rapper's Delight
composer: Sylvia Robinson, Wonder Mike, Big Bank Hank, Master Gee (interpolating Chic's 'Good Times')
recordingNote: Debut single, released in 1979 on Sugar Hill Records, produced by Sylvia Robinson
context: "Rapper's Delight" was the debut single of the Sugarhill Gang, a New Jersey trio assembled by producer Sylvia Robinson. Recorded in 1979 over a replayed bassline from Chic's "Good Times", it is credited with introducing rap music to a wide audience: it reached the US top 40, went top three in the UK and hit number one in Canada. Though the Fatback Band's "King Tim III" came first, this is the record that took hip hop national.
listenFor: The looping Chic bassline rolling under Wonder Mike's opening "I said a hip hop, the hippie..." — the moment rap first reached the mainstream.

title: The Message
composer: Duke Bootee, Melle Mel, Clifton Chase, Sylvia Robinson
recordingNote: Written in 1980; released as a single on Sugar Hill Records on July 1, 1982, later the title track of the group's debut album
context: Written in 1980 by Duke Bootee and Melle Mel in response to the New York City transit strike, "The Message" was released by Sugar Hill Records on July 1, 1982. Where earlier rap records centred the party, it painted broken elevators, dead-end jobs and urban decay, and it is widely credited with opening hip hop's socially conscious tradition. It became the group's signature record and a blueprint for every storyteller MC who followed.
listenFor: The eerie synthesiser bubbling under the famous opening line — "don't push me 'cause I am close to the edge" — hip hop's first great chorus of desperation.

title: Walk This Way
recordingNote: Run-DMC's remake with Steven Tyler and Joe Perry, from Raising Hell (1986); original written and released by Aerosmith in 1975
context: Aerosmith wrote "Walk This Way" in 1975 and it was a top ten hit for them two years later. In 1986 Run-DMC rebuilt it from drum machine and guitar riff, trading verses with Steven Tyler and Joe Perry for the Raising Hell album. The collaboration put rap in heavy rotation on MTV, introduced hip hop to a rock audience, and revitalised Aerosmith's own career in the process.
listenFor: The drum machine alone for a full verse before Joe Perry's guitar crashes in — the sound of two genres meeting halfway.

title: Fight the Power
composer: Chuck D, Public Enemy (production: The Bomb Squad)
recordingNote: Released summer 1989 on Motown for Spike Lee's Do the Right Thing; extended version on Fear of a Black Planet (1990)
context: Spike Lee asked Public Enemy for a musical theme for his 1989 film Do the Right Thing, and Chuck D answered with "Fight the Power", released in summer 1989 on Motown. The extended version anchored the group's third album Fear of a Black Planet (1990). Built on the Bomb Squad's dense collage of samples and voices, it remains the group's defining statement — a demand, not a request.
listenFor: The layers of found sound — horns, shouts, Flavor Flav's heckling — stacking on top of each other like a street protest with a beat.

title: Can I Kick It?
composer: A Tribe Called Quest (samples Lou Reed's 'Walk on the Wild Side')
recordingNote: Recorded in 1989; released October 1990 on Jive Records as the third single from People's Instinctive Travels and the Paths of Rhythm
context: Released in October 1990 on Jive as the third single from People's Instinctive Travels and the Paths of Rhythm, "Can I Kick It?" was recorded in 1989, when Q-Tip and Phife Dawg were just 18 and 19. Its call-and-response chorus became a live staple, and its laid-back loop of Lou Reed's "Walk on the Wild Side" helped define the warm, jazzy, sample-driven sound of early-1990s alternative hip hop.
listenFor: The slinky Lou Reed bassline answered by the crowd's "yes you can" — call and response you can't help joining.

title: C.R.E.A.M.
composer: RZA, Raekwon, Inspectah Deck, Method Man (sampling the Charmels)
recordingNote: From Enter the Wu-Tang (36 Chambers) (1993); released as a single on Loud Records on January 31, 1994
context: "C.R.E.A.M." — cash rules everything around me — was the second single from Wu-Tang Clan's 1993 debut Enter the Wu-Tang (36 Chambers), released on Loud Records on January 31, 1994. Produced by RZA around a loop of the Charmels' 1967 single "As Long As I've Got You", it pairs Raekwon's and Inspectah Deck's verses about growing up in New York with Method Man's mournful sung hook, and it put the Clan on the map.
listenFor: The ghostly 1967 soul loop, cold piano notes and all, that RZA lets run untouched beneath the hardest verses of 1993.

title: Juicy
recordingNote: First single from Ready to Die (1994); produced by Poke of Trackmasters and Sean Combs
context: "Juicy" was the first single from The Notorious B.I.G.'s debut album Ready to Die (1994), produced by Poke of the Trackmasters and Sean Combs. It flips Mtume's 1983 hit "Juicy Fruit" into a rags-to-riches story that climbs from a shot-up apartment to penthouse views, and it is widely considered one of the greatest hip hop tracks of all time. It announced Biggie as a storyteller of rare warmth and wit.
listenFor: The Mtume chorus melting into the verse — "it was all a dream" — nostalgia and celebration riding the same beat.

title: Doo Wop (That Thing)
recordingNote: Written and produced by Hill; lead single from The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill, released August 10, 1998
context: Lauryn Hill wrote and produced "Doo Wop (That Thing)" herself and released it on August 10, 1998 as her solo debut and the lead single from The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill. Over a beat that nods to 1960s doo-wop, she spends one verse calling out materialistic men and the next doing the same to the women chasing them — equal-opportunity tough love, delivered in a singing rap that switches lanes mid-bar.
listenFor: The two halves of the song — one side of the record smooth and soulful, the other all hip hop swagger — meeting in the middle.

title: Alright
composer: Kendrick Lamar, Pharrell Williams, Pharrell co-production (To Pimp a Butterfly)
recordingNote: From To Pimp a Butterfly (2015); released as the album's fourth single on June 30, 2015, co-produced by Pharrell Williams
context: "Alright" appears on Kendrick Lamar's 2015 album To Pimp a Butterfly and was released as its fourth single on June 30, 2015, co-produced by Pharrell Williams, who also sings the chorus. The song expresses hope amid personal struggle, and many publications ranked it among the best songs and videos of the year. It received four nominations at the 58th Grammy Awards, including Song of the Year and Best Music Video.
listenFor: Pharrell's voice lifting the chorus — hard times on every side, and still "we gon' be alright" — against the album's darker, jazz-heavy verses.

title: Denial Is a River
composer: Doechii (produced by Ian James, Joey Hamhock, Banser)
recordingNote: From the mixtape Alligator Bites Never Heal (2024); released to radio as its third single on January 28, 2025
context: Tampa rapper Doechii released "Denial Is a River" on her second mixtape, Alligator Bites Never Heal (2024), and pushed it to pop and rhythmic radio as the third single on January 28, 2025. Produced by Ian James, Joey Hamhock and Banser, it stages a therapy-session monologue over a swaggering boom-bap beat, and it reached the top ten in both the United Kingdom and New Zealand.
listenFor: The comic back-and-forth voices — therapist, inner child, phone call — skits riding inside the verse like a radio drama over boom bap.

title: West End Blues
performer: Louis Armstrong and His Hot Five
recordingNote: The June 28, 1928 Chicago recording for Okeh by Louis Armstrong and His Hot Five — the best-known version of the tune
context: King Oliver wrote this twelve-bar blues and first recorded it on June 11, 1928; seventeen days later his former protégé Louis Armstrong cut the version everyone remembers, for Okeh on June 28, 1928. The Hot Five that day included Earl Hines on piano and drummer Zutty Singleton. Armstrong's unaccompanied opening cadenza was unlike anything on record at the time, and the record entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1979.
listenFor: The unaccompanied trumpet cadenza in the first twelve seconds — Armstrong jumps in alone before the band arrives — then the hushed scat duet with Jimmy Strong's low clarinet.

title: Sing, Sing, Sing (With a Swing)
recordingNote: The extended 8:43 instrumental recorded in Hollywood on July 6, 1937, arranged by Jimmy Mundy and released on both sides of a 12-inch 78
context: Louis Prima wrote and first recorded this song in 1936, but it became the Benny Goodman Orchestra's signature. Recorded in Hollywood on July 6, 1937 with Gene Krupa on drums and Harry James on trumpet, it ran 8 minutes 43 seconds — far past the three-minute norm for 78s — with arranger Jimmy Mundy folding in Chu Berry's "Christopher Columbus". It entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1982.
listenFor: Gene Krupa's drumming pushing the band past where the tune was supposed to end, and Jess Stacy's quiet, almost thought-out piano solo near the close.

title: Ko-Ko
recordingNote: The original Savoy master, recorded November 26, 1945 at WOR studios, New York City
context: Recorded November 26, 1945 at WOR studios in New York for the Savoy label, "Ko-Ko" is built on the chord changes of "Cherokee". Bud Powell was absent from the session, so Dizzy Gillespie took the piano chair while young Miles Davis played trumpet, with Curley Russell on bass and Max Roach on drums. The Library of Congress added the recording to the National Recording Registry in 2002.
listenFor: Max Roach's drum interlude splitting the two sax-and-trumpet choruses, and how the tune never once states a written melody — it's all improvisation on the "Cherokee" changes.

title: Strange Fruit
recordingNote: The April 20, 1939 Commodore recording, with Frankie Newton's Café Society Band and Sonny White's piano introduction
context: Abel Meeropol wrote this protest against lynching as a poem, and Billie Holiday first sang it at Café Society, New York's first integrated nightclub. Columbia refused to record it, so she cut it for Milt Gabler's Commodore label on April 20, 1939, with Frankie Newton's eight-piece Café Society Band. Gabler had pianist Sonny White improvise an intro, so Holiday doesn't sing until about 70 seconds in. The 1939 recording sold a million copies and entered the National Recording Registry in 2003.
listenFor: The long solo-piano introduction holding the room silent, then the bareness of Holiday's voice carrying the whole weight of the lyric.

title: So What
recordingNote: Opening track of Kind of Blue, recorded March 2, 1959 for Columbia
context: Recorded March 2, 1959, this is the first track of Kind of Blue, the album Miles Davis made with John Coltrane, Cannonball Adderley, Bill Evans, Paul Chambers, and Jimmy Cobb. Gil Evans wrote the piano-and-bass introduction heard at the start, written out for Bill Evans and Paul Chambers. The whole piece moves between just two chords a half-step apart, and the answering figures Davis plays behind Coltrane and Adderley gave pianists what's now called the "So What chord".
listenFor: Bill Evans and Paul Chambers stating the theme in unison at the top, then Davis soloing over one chord for nearly a minute without losing your attention.

title: Goodbye Pork Pie Hat
recordingNote: From the 1959 Columbia album Mingus Ah Um, played by Mingus's sextet
context: Mingus wrote this slow, mournful theme for saxophonist Lester Young, who had died two months before the Mingus Ah Um recording sessions — the pork pie hat was Young's trademark. The 1959 sextet version features John Handy and Booker Ervin on tenor saxophones, Horace Parlan on piano, and Mingus's own bass out front. It became one of his most covered compositions, later reworked with lyrics by Joni Mitchell on her 1979 album Mingus.
listenFor: Mingus's bass carrying the melody at the start, then John Handy's tenor picking up the tune with a vocal, faltering quality that suits the elegy.

title: Journey in Satchidananda
recordingNote: Title track of the Impulse! album released February 1971, recorded November 8, 1970 at Coltrane's home studio in Dix Hills, New York
context: Alice Coltrane recorded this in November 1970 at her home studio in Dix Hills, New York, for her fourth Impulse! album, released in February 1971. Her harp and piano are joined by Pharoah Sanders on saxophone, Cecil McBee on bass, Rashied Ali on drums, Majid Shabazz on percussion, and a droning tanpura — the title honors Swami Satchidananda, whom she had studied under. Rolling Stone ranked the album number 446 on its 2020 list of the 500 greatest albums.
listenFor: The tanpura's steady drone under Coltrane's harp, with Pharoah Sanders' soprano sax circling above it — less a chord progression than a continuous hum.

title: Mannenberg
recordingNote: Recorded in June 1974 in a Cape Town studio, released under the name Dollar Brand on the album Mannenberg – Is Where It's Happening
context: Abdullah Ibrahim — then recording as Dollar Brand — cut this in a Cape Town studio in June 1974, produced by Rashid Vally, during one of the brief visits home his exiled status allowed. Basil Coetzee's saxophone solo was so central that he took "Manenberg" as a nickname. Drawing on the Cape Town street styles of marabi and langarm, it sold tens of thousands of copies within months and became an unofficial anthem of the anti-apartheid movement in the 1980s.
listenFor: The rolling, dancing piano figure Ibrahim plays almost from the first bar — a rhythm you could walk to — before Coetzee's saxophone enters and lifts it.

title: Kogun
performer: Toshiko Akiyoshi – Lew Tabackin Big Band
recordingNote: Title track of Kogun, the band's first album, recorded April 3–4, 1974 at Sage & Sand Studio, Hollywood
context: Pianist and composer Toshiko Akiyoshi formed this sixteen-piece band in Los Angeles in 1973 with her husband, saxophonist Lew Tabackin, and recorded its first album at Sage & Sand Studio in Hollywood in April 1974. The title track takes its name — "a lone army" — from Hiroo Onoda, the Japanese soldier who held out in the Philippine jungle for decades after the war ended. The album won Japan's Swing Journal Silver Disk prize and earned a 1979 Grammy nomination.
listenFor: The group's No-theater-inspired chanting and kotsuzumi-style drum sounds folded into a full big band — Akiyoshi weaving Japanese color through American orchestral jazz.

title: Afro Blue
performer: Robert Glasper Experiment feat. Erykah Badu
recordingNote: From the Blue Note album Black Radio, released February 28, 2012, with Erykah Badu singing Oscar Brown Jr.'s lyrics
context: Conguero Mongo Santamaría composed "Afro Blue" in 1959 as an instrumental — the first jazz standard built on a 3:2 African cross-rhythm — and Oscar Brown Jr. added lyrics that same year. Pianist Robert Glasper and his electric quartet recast it with Erykah Badu's voice for Black Radio, released February 28, 2012 on Blue Note. The album won the Grammy for Best R&B Album in 2013, with Casey Benjamin on vocoder and saxophone, Derrick Hodge on bass, and Chris Dave on drums.
listenFor: The lilting 6/8 swing that never speeds up under Badu's unhurried vocal, and Casey Benjamin's vocoder answers floating behind her.

title: I'm Waiting for the Man
recordingNote: Recorded May 1966 at TTG Studios, Hollywood; official Universal Music Group audio from The Velvet Underground & Nico 45th Anniversary (Super Deluxe Edition)
context: Recorded in May 1966 at TTG Studios in Hollywood and released on Verve on 12 March 1967, this is Lou Reed's unsentimental story of riding the subway to Harlem to buy heroin — a plain-spoken drug song on a major label, with Andy Warhol credited as producer. Critics file it among the founding documents of proto-punk, a garage-rock stomper years ahead of the punk wave it helped start.
listenFor: The relentless piano vamp hammering away under Reed's deadpan vocal, never once resolving into a chorus.

title: "Heroes"
recordingNote: Recorded July–August 1977 at Hansa by the Wall, West Berlin; official HD video from David Bowie's channel (2018)
context: Written with Brian Eno and produced by Bowie and Tony Visconti, "Heroes" was recorded in July and August 1977 at Hansa Studios in West Berlin, close to the Wall, and released as a single on 23 September 1977. The album version stretches past six minutes; the single was trimmed to 3:32 — a love song shot through the cold of the city's divided, art-rock years.
listenFor: Bowie's voice climbing an octave higher with each repeat of "I, I will be king".

title: London Calling
recordingNote: From the December 1979 double album London Calling; official video on the theclashVEVO channel (2009 upload)
context: The Clash's apocalyptic opener was recorded at Wessex Studios in a former church hall in North London and released as a single on 7 December 1979, ahead of the double album of the same name. Its title echoes the BBC World Service announcement "This is London calling", and its ice-age imagery was partly spurred by the March 1979 Three Mile Island nuclear accident. It reached No. 11 in the UK and entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2007.
listenFor: Paul Simonon's descending bass line pulling the song in before Strummer's hoarse warning arrives.

title: Where Is My Mind?
recordingNote: Original recording 1988 on Surfer Rosa; official 4AD audio upload (the Death to the Pixies compilation version)
context: The closing track on Surfer Rosa, the Pixies' 1988 debut album, "Where Is My Mind?" became the band's signature song after its use in the 1999 film Fight Club brought it a second life. It has since drawn a multitude of covers and turned up across film, television and games, outgrowing every other song in the Boston band's catalogue.
listenFor: The woozy lead guitar wandering off-key while Kim Deal's backing "oohs" circle the chorus.

title: Paranoid Android
recordingNote: Lead single from OK Computer, released 26 May 1997 on Parlophone; official video on Radiohead's channel (2015 upload)
context: Six and a half minutes and four distinct sections, released as the lead single from OK Computer on 26 May 1997 — "Paranoid Android" took its title from Marvin in The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, its lyrics from a hostile night Thom Yorke experienced in a Los Angeles bar. It reached No. 3 in the UK, and Magnus Carlsson's surreal animated video got heavy MTV rotation.
listenFor: The gear-change when Jonny Greenwood's guitar solo erupts after the second "rain down" section.

title: Seven Nation Army
recordingNote: Lead single from Elephant, released 17 February 2003 on V2/XL; official video on The White Stripes channel (2008 upload)
context: Jack White sketched the famous riff at a soundcheck at Melbourne's Corner Hotel in January 2002, playing a semi-acoustic guitar through an octave pedal — there is no bass guitar anywhere on the recording. Released 17 February 2003 as the lead single from Elephant, it won the 2004 Grammy for Best Rock Song and became a global sports anthem, especially around the 2018 World Cup.
listenFor: The growling octave-pedal riff standing alone at the start until the drums crash in behind it.

title: Rebellion (Lies)
composer: Win Butler, Régine Chassagne, Tim Kingsbury, Richard Reed Parry & Howard Bilerman
recordingNote: From Funeral, released 14 September 2004 on Merge Records; official remastered video on ArcadeFireVEVO (2019 upload)
context: From Funeral, Arcade Fire's debut album — released through Merge Records on 14 September 2004, shadowed by the deaths of several band members' relatives during its making — "Rebellion (Lies)" followed as its fourth single on 12 September 2005. It outdid the album's other singles in the UK, reaching No. 19, and has become the band's most-performed live song.
listenFor: The driving piano figure and Régine Chassagne's wordless high vocal pushing the song toward its final surge.

title: Do I Wanna Know?
recordingNote: Lead single from AM, released on Domino in June 2013; official video on the Arctic Monkeys channel
context: David Wilson's animated video for "Do I Wanna Know?" went up on YouTube on 18 June 2013 and had passed a billion views by June 2020 — one of only twelve rock videos to get there. It introduced Arctic Monkeys' fifth album, AM, released later that year on Domino, with James Ford and Ross Orton producing Alex Turner's turn toward slow-burn, heavy-groove songwriting.
listenFor: The woozy lead-guitar line that answers Turner's opening question like a second voice.

title: Masseduction
recordingNote: Title track of MASSEDUCTION, released 13 October 2017 on Loma Vista; official video on St. Vincent's channel (2019 upload)
context: The title track of St. Vincent's fifth album, MASSEDUCTION, made with producer Jack Antonoff and released on Loma Vista on 13 October 2017, "Masseduction" won Best Rock Song at the 2019 Grammy Awards. Annie Clark framed the record around what she called "sex and drugs and sadness", and it became her first US top-ten album, reaching No. 10 on the Billboard 200.
listenFor: Clark's electric-guitar solo slicing through the glossy synth-pop sheen near the end.

title: Starburster
recordingNote: Lead single from Romance, released 17 April 2024 on XL Recordings; official video on the Fontaines DC channel
context: Fontaines D.C. released "Starburster" on 17 April 2024 as the lead single from Romance, their fourth album and first for XL Recordings. Frontman Grian Chatten wrote it in the grip of a panic attack suffered at London's St Pancras station, and the track's gasping intake of breath drives its hip-hop-adjacent rhythm. It became the Irish band's first UK charting single, peaking at No. 57.
listenFor: The sharp gasp of breath that opens the track and keeps returning like a skipped heartbeat.
